1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / partially reported at initiative level: refusal and non-participation rates among approached key informants are not reported; case selection targeted already-sustained ('surviving') initiatives, though participant dropout is noted qualitatively in one case study (Warren Park 2 garden membership dropout after external funding ended and land lease fees became unaffordable, Table 3, PDF Page 7).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern for causal attribution (not applicable as a formal statistical domain in descriptive qualitative synthesis): no comparator sites or counterfactual designs were used, and observed social, material, and health improvements across complex multi-actor urban initiatives cannot be separated from concurrent municipal, donor, or socio-economic changes, as the authors acknowledge (PDF Page 14).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak (descriptive secondary reporting only): legal, regulatory, and tenure dimensions—such as contested land lacking legal title in Hatcliffe, 5-year municipal leases in Warren Park 2, missing post-2006 legal mandates for neighbourhood health committees in Lusaka, county urban agriculture laws and a Special Planning Area / MoU in Nairobi, and Uganda's Ministry of Lands Housing and Urban Development community contracting guidelines—are summarized briefly from case reports without statutory citations, doctrinal verification, or systematic legal coding (Tables 3–4, PDF Pages 7–9, 12–14).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: findings rely on secondary published/grey project documents and 34 key informant interviews without reported interview guides, recording/transcription procedures, or verbatim participant quotes in the article; insider affiliation of local 'focal person' co-authors and the EQUINET network with studied initiatives introduces potential social desirability and interpretive bias.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (unverified secondary narrative reporting): water, sanitation, waste, and health outcomes (e.g., pilot water-conserving toilets in 30 Epworth households, community water-testing attitudes, solid-waste briquette recycling in Bwaise, and general references to routine clinic data showing reduced communicable/epidemic disease) are reported narratively without standardized WASH definitions, microbiological/physical measurements, or baseline-to-endline quantitative data (PDF Pages 5–10, Tables 3–4).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: although NYU IRB clearance was obtained, no pre-registered study protocol or coding codebook is cited, primary interview transcripts/quotations are omitted in favour of high-level synthesis deferring to external grey reports (refs. 27–31), and English-only published sources may under-report failed initiatives, though Table 3 explicitly tabulates implementation barriers alongside enablers.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern (purposive positive-case selection): the desk review was restricted to post-2010 English-language documents without snowballing, and the 4 cities and 10 case studies were purposively chosen specifically because they had published reports of sustained initiatives with positive outcomes; furthermore, sampling criteria, stakeholder roles, and per-site counts for the 34 key informants are unreported.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its aim to document and understand the features of urban initiatives, practices, and processes in East and Southern Africa (ESA) that promote health and wellbeing and how they contribute to five dimensions of equity (participatory, recognitional, distributional, structural, and intergenerational), situating this aim against an explicit literature gap in ESA urban health equity practice.

A qualitative approach (focused document review, structured multi-site case studies, key informant interviews, and thematic content analysis) is appropriate for exploring complex contextual processes, multi-actor governance dynamics, and qualitative equity dimensions across diverse non-biomedical urban social-determinant initiatives.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly justify combining a broad regional focused narrative review across 16 EQUINET ESA countries (52 included papers) with 10 purposively selected city case studies (Harare, Kampala, Lusaka, Nairobi) drawing on 122 published/grey documents and 34 key informant interviews (Figure 1) to capture both regional breadth and deeper process learning, explaining why a focused review and case-study content analysis suited multivariate qualitative evidence better than a biomedical systematic review.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Sources of evidence and Figure 1 (PDF Pages 2–4)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: While the purposive selection of four cities and 10 sustained positive-outcome initiatives is explained (to learn from promising practice within resource constraints, assisted by local urban health 'focal persons'), the paper provides insufficient detail on how the 34 key informants were selected and recruited—omitting per-case sample sizes, informant categories (e.g., programme implementers vs. municipal officials vs. community residents), inclusion criteria, and non-response/refusal rates, while noting in Limitations that insights came particularly from implementers.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Sources of evidence and Limitations (PDF Pages 3–5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Although desk search databases/terms (May 2022) and the thematic domains extracted across the 10 case studies (June–July 2022) are outlined, critical primary data collection details for the 34 key informant interviews are omitted from this article (deferred to external grey reports 27–31): no interview guide is presented, interview modality/setting, duration, audio-recording vs. note-taking, transcription procedures, and thematic saturation are unreported, and the authors note time/resource limits precluded wider field interviews, focus groups, and direct observations.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Sources of evidence and Limitations (PDF Pages 3–5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Reflexivity and researcher positionality are not critically examined despite clear insider relationships: the four city 'focal persons' involved in Urban Health who selected and implemented the case studies and conducted key informant interviews (DG, FG, CW, SC) are co-authors, and the sponsoring network (EQUINET, led by first author RL) was directly involved in supporting and documenting studied initiatives (e.g., the Lusaka primary health care participation initiative, Table 3 and refs. 34, 35, 64). No discussion addresses how these dual roles influenced case selection, informant candour, or interpretation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Sources of evidence (PDF Page 3); Table 3 (PDF Page 7); Author contributions and Acknowledgments (PDF Page 16)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Even though secondary document review was public domain, the authors submitted the study protocol through the International Society for Urban Health (ISUH) to the New York University IRB and received ethical clearance, obtained standard informed consent via focal persons prior to all key informant interviews, and anonymised key informants.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: While the deductive-inductive thematic structure (four cross-cutting areas and five equity dimensions) and co-author/stakeholder review are stated, the mechanics of manual content analysis (carried out by RL per Author contributions) lack a coding codebook, audit trail, or independent double-coding check. Moreover, zero verbatim quotes from the 34 key informants are presented in the Results to substantiate interpretations with primary empirical data, relying entirely on narrative summaries and citations to external reports.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Analysis of the evidence (PDF Pages 4–5); Results (PDF Pages 5–11); Author contributions (PDF Page 16)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized across focus areas, social/material/health outcomes, cross-case enablers and barriers (Table 3), and the five-dimensional equity framework (Table 4), explicitly noting methodological limitations, evidence gaps in distributional and structural equity, and validation with key informants and a regional review meeting.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results (PDF Pages 5–11, Tables 1–3); Discussion (PDF Pages 11–16, Table 4); Limitations (PDF Page 5)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: The study offers a valuable conceptual and practical synthesis of how community-facing urban initiatives across East and Southern Africa (spanning water and sanitation, solid waste and flood management, urban agriculture, public spaces, and primary health care) operationalize recognitional and participatory equity as levers for broader wellbeing, while identifying actionable gaps in routine intra-urban disaggregated monitoring and higher-level legal/structural reform.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable synthesis with transferable regional insights (narrative assessment)
domain_ratings.where_found: Discussion — Learning and insights on improving urban health equity (PDF Pages 11–16)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Loewenson et al. (2023) is a multi-method qualitative study combining a focused (explicitly non-systematic) narrative desk review of 52 post-2010 English-language documents across 16 East and Southern African countries with 10 purposively selected city case studies (Harare, Kampala, Lusaka, and Nairobi) informed by 122 published/grey documents and 34 IRB-cleared key informant interviews, synthesized via manual thematic content analysis across five equity dimensions. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study demonstrates clear research aims (Q1: Yes), an appropriate qualitative multi-case design (Q2: Yes; Q3: Yes), documented NYU IRB clearance, informed consent, and informant anonymisation (Q7: Yes), and well-structured cross-case findings (Q9: Yes) with substantial regional policy relevance (Q10). However, there is moderate methodological concern overall (3 'Can't tell' items and 1 'No' item): recruitment details and stakeholder composition/refusals for the 34 key informants are unreported in this paper (Q4: Can't tell); primary interview procedures (interview guide, recording/transcription, saturation) are omitted and field focus groups/observations were precluded by resource constraints (Q5: Can't tell); researcher reflexivity is absent despite city focal persons and the sponsoring EQUINET network having direct involvement in selecting, implementing, or supporting studied initiatives (Q6: No); and manual coding was conducted by one lead author without a reported codebook or primary verbatim participant quotes in the text (Q8: Can't tell). Legal/institutional features and WASH/health outcomes are summarized descriptively from secondary reports without primary doctrinal or quantitative verification.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (3 Can't tell items, 1 No item)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Multi-method qualitative study combining a focused narrative document review (52 papers across 16 East and Southern African countries) with 10 purposively selected qualitative city case studies (122 published/grey documents and 34 key informant interviews in Harare, Kampala, Lusaka, and Nairobi), synthesized via manual thematic content analysis
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Introduction (PDF Page 2); Methods — Sources of evidence, Figure 1, Table 1, Table 2, Analysis of the evidence, and Limitations (PDF Pages 2–5); Results and Table 3 (PDF Pages 5–11); Discussion and Table 4 (PDF Pages 11–16); Author contributions and Acknowledgments (PDF Page 16).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Although published under Frontiers in Public Health's 'Policy and Practice Reviews' rubric, the authors explicitly state they conducted a non-systematic focused narrative review rather than a systematic review (ruling out AMSTAR 2) combined with 10 primary qualitative documentary and key-informant interview case studies (34 interviews, IRB-cleared) analysed via manual thematic content analysis without any quantitative empirical study component (ruling out MMAT). The CASP Qualitative Checklist is therefore the exact matching instrument for this qualitative documentary and interview case-study synthesis.
